questions.stem: A 64-year-old man presented with acutely altered mental status. The patient’s family reported that the patient had been confused for 1–2 days and had been walking into walls. He had a history of hypertension, diabetes mellitus, hyperlipidemia, and poor dentition. He had no known drug allergies. Physical exam revealed mild left hemiparesis and decreased left temporal visual field. Investigations: Total white cell count 13,300 cells/mm3 Serum creatinine 1.05 mg/dL Normal liver function tests MRI brain: 4 ×3 cm rim-enhancing lesion in the right parieto-occipital region. The patient was taken to the operating room, where frank pus was drained from the mass. Gram-stain of the abscess fluid: abundant gram-positive cocci in pairs and chains on direct microscopy; culture revealed viridans group streptococci.
questions.lead_in: What beta-lactam would be most appropriate to include in this patient’s antibiotic regimen?
questions.explanation: Ceftriaxone Cefazolin does not adequately penetrate the blood–brain barrier and is not appropriate for treatment of central nervous system infections. Cefepime and ceftazidime are established treatments for gram-negative central nervous system infections but offer no advantage over ceftriaxone for coverage of viridans group streptococci. Cefotetan is not established for treatment of central nervous system infections. Ceftriaxone is considered a therapy of choice for central nervous system infections caused by viridans group streptococcus.

questions.model_answer: a) Diagnosis: MRI with gadolinium is the first imaging choice – a ring-enhancing lesion with central diffusion restriction on DWI (low ADC) is characteristic of a pyogenic abscess and distinguishes it from cystic tumour. Proceed to stereotactic CT/MRI-guided aspiration (all lesions >2.5 cm) to obtain pus. Microbiology request on the aspirate: Gram stain; routine aerobic AND anaerobic cultures; mycobacterial and fungal cultures/special stains; and 16S rRNA gene PCR/sequencing (useful if cultures are negative). Also draw blood cultures (yield up to 28%). b) A temporal-lobe abscess typically arises from an otitic focus, so cover streptococci (incl. S. anginosus group), anaerobes (Bacteroides/Prevotella) and Enterobacteriaceae: metronidazole 30 mg/kg/day IV divided q6h (e.g. 500 mg q6–8h) + a third-generation cephalosporin (ceftriaxone 2 g IV q12h [4 g/day] or cefotaxime 8–12 g/day q4–6h). If pathogenesis is unclear, add vancomycin 30–45 mg/kg/day q8–12h. Continue IV therapy 6–8 weeks with serial neuroimaging.

questions.model_answer: a) (1) Contiguous spread – otitis media/mastoiditis (streptococci, Bacteroides/Prevotella, Enterobacteriaceae), paranasal sinusitis (streptococci, Bacteroides, Enterobacteriaceae, S. aureus, Haemophilus), dental infection (Fusobacterium, Prevotella, Actinomyces, Bacteroides, streptococci). (2) Hematogenous from a distant focus – lung abscess/empyema/bronchiectasis (Fusobacterium, Actinomyces, Bacteroides/Prevotella, streptococci, Nocardia), endocarditis (S. aureus, streptococci), cyanotic congenital heart disease (streptococci, Haemophilus). (3) Trauma/post-neurosurgical – S. aureus, streptococci, Enterobacteriaceae, Clostridium. b) Otitis/sinusitis/dental: metronidazole + third-generation cephalosporin (cefotaxime/ceftriaxone). Trauma/post-neurosurgical: vancomycin + third/fourth-generation cephalosporin. Lung source: third-generation cephalosporin + metronidazole + a sulfonamide (TMP-SMX for Nocardia). Endocarditis: vancomycin. Unknown: vancomycin + metronidazole + third/fourth-generation cephalosporin. Agents that do NOT cross the BBB / should be avoided: echinocandins (caspofungin) do not cross the BBB; posaconazole has poor CNS penetration; aminoglycosides penetrate poorly. c) Surgical indications: any ring-enhancing lesion >2.5 cm (aspirate/excise); need for microbiologic diagnosis; multiloculated abscess or aspiration failure; gas-containing abscess; failure to resolve / enlargement after 1–2 weeks of therapy; posttraumatic abscess with foreign body or retained bone fragments; abscess from a fistulous communication; increased ICP/impending herniation; intraventricular rupture (ventricular drainage). d) MRSA coverage (vancomycin): suspected/proven S. aureus – cranial trauma, post-neurosurgical, infective endocarditis, community-associated MRSA risk. Pseudomonas coverage (ceftazidime or cefepime): post-neurosurgical, chronic otitic focus, and immunocompromised/neutropenic hosts. e) Concurrent brain + lung: Nocardia spp. (TMP-SMX/sulfonamide; alt minocycline, imipenem/meropenem, linezolid, amikacin), Actinomyces (penicillin G), and Aspergillus spp. (voriconazole) – lungs are the usual primary site.

questions.model_answer: a) Odontogenic (dental-source) bacterial brain abscess – typically Streptococcus anginosus group and oral anaerobes. b) MRI with gadolinium (with DWI) to confirm, then stereotactic CT/MRI-guided aspiration with specimen for Gram stain, aerobic/anaerobic cultures and 16S PCR; blood cultures; dental examination/Panorex to identify the source; CT chest and echocardiography to exclude metastatic/embolic foci; consider HIV testing. c) Common metastatic abscess sites for S. anginosus group: (1) liver abscess and (2) thoracic empyema (endocarditis is another recognized complication).
questions.beyond_mandell: The S. anginosus group's proclivity for metastatic liver abscess/empyema/endocarditis is general knowledge (see Mandell Ch. 203); this chapter notes only that these organisms reside in the oral cavity and form abscesses.

cohort_answer.text:
Diagnosis: Odontogenic brain abscess (per subsequent slide heading 'Odotogenic brain abscess').
Investigations: Blood cultures, Echo, Dental exam/Panorex, HIV test, CXR.
Two common sites of metastases: Endocarditis, Liver abscess (for S. anginosus), Empyema, Acute bacterial sialadenitis, Peritonitis.

questions.model_answer: a) Frontal lobe is the predominant site for abscess arising from the paranasal (frontoethmoid) sinuses; dental infection of a molar is the other classic frontal-lobe source. Most likely primary site: frontoethmoid paranasal sinus (or odontogenic). b) For a sinusitis/dental source: metronidazole 30 mg/kg/day IV divided q6h + third-generation cephalosporin (ceftriaxone 2 g IV q12h or cefotaxime 8–12 g/day); add vancomycin 30–45 mg/kg/day q8–12h if MRSA possible or source unclear. c) Group: Streptococcus anginosus (milleri) group. Three members: (1) Streptococcus anginosus (2) Streptococcus constellatus (3) Streptococcus intermedius.

cohort_answer.text: Primary site: Frontal or ethmoid sinuses. Brain abscess: haematogenous (usually multiple) or direct spread (usually single abscess), post NSx procedure, foreign body, facial trauma. Empiric treatment: CTX 2g IV q12hr (meningeal dosing) + vanco + metro. Organism group: S. anginosus group. Members: S. anginosus; S. intermedius; S. constellatus.

questions.model_answer: a) Cellulitis: 5 days (extend only if not improving). b) Acute uncomplicated pyelonephritis: 5 days (levofloxacin) – 7 days for ciprofloxacin. c) CAP: minimum 5 days (afebrile 48–72 h, clinically stable). d) VAP: 7 days. e) Frontal brain abscess: 6–8 weeks of IV therapy is traditional; a shorter 3–4 week course may be adequate when the abscess has been surgically excised.
questions.beyond_mandell: Durations for cellulitis, pyelonephritis, CAP and VAP are from IDSA guidance (IDSA SSTI 2014; IDSA/ATS HAP/VAP 2016; IDSA/ATS CAP 2019), not this chapter.

questions.model_answer: a) Immunocompromised host (hematologic malignancy / cellular immune defect) with concurrent cavitary lung lesions and brain abscess points to pathogens that disseminate hematogenously from the lung to the CNS. Three organisms with empiric therapy: (1) Nocardia spp. — high-dose trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole plus a carbapenem (imipenem or meropenem), often with amikacin for serious/CNS disease; (2) Aspergillus spp. — voriconazole; (3) Mycobacterium tuberculosis — four-drug therapy (isoniazid, rifampin, ethambutol, pyrazinamide) with corticosteroids. In practice, while awaiting aspiration/culture, many experts treat an immunocompromised patient empirically with high-dose meropenem (covers Nocardia, anaerobes, gram-negative bacilli including Pseudomonas, and possibly Listeria) plus voriconazole plus vancomycin (until MRSA excluded). (Other acceptable organisms: Cryptococcus neoformans — liposomal amphotericin B + flucytosine; or Candida spp. in neutropenia.)
questions.beyond_mandell: Specific Nocardia regimen (TMP-SMX + carbapenem ± amikacin) and standard RIPE + steroids for TB follow IDSA/standard guidance; the chapter names the organisms and the meropenem + voriconazole + vancomycin empiric combination.

cohort_answer.text: Nocardia: TMP/SMX + imipenem/meropenem + amikacin. Aspergillus: Voriconazole. Tuberculosis: INH/RIF/ETH/PYZ + steroids. Cryptococcus neoformans: Amphotericin B + Flucytosine (treatment phase) → Fluconazole (consolidation and suppressive phases). Actinomyces (A. meyeri, odontolyticus, israelii): Penicillin + surgery for CNS. Streptococcus anginosus: Ceftriaxone. S. aureus: Vancomycin.

parts.text: State the virulence factors that allow the causative organism to produce this specific clinical picture.

parts_raw.text: B) Virulence factors for organism that cause this specific clinical picture?

questions.model_answer: Organism: hypervirulent Klebsiella pneumoniae causing Klebsiella liver abscess with metastatic (brain abscess/meningitis) spread. Virulence factors: (1) Hypermucoviscous polysaccharide capsule, chiefly serotype K1 (and K2), inhibiting phagocytosis and resisting complement/serum killing, linked to clonal complex CC23 carrying a virulence plasmid. (2) rmpA (regulator of mucoid phenotype) driving the hypermucoviscous string-test-positive phenotype (magA is a K1 marker rather than an independent driver). (3) Aerobactin and other TonB-regulated siderophore iron-acquisition systems supporting invasive/metastatic disease. (4) Types 1 and 3 fimbriae for host-cell adherence.
